source.title: Honey, I Shrunk the Language: Language Model Behavior at Reduced Scale
source.authors: Vijeta Deshpande; Dan Pechi; Shree Thatte; V. Lialin; Anna Rumshisky

record.tranche_reason: The study measures MLM loss against model size, data size and FLOPs in a reduced-vocabulary, small-model setting, and reports a low-compute departure from a power curve.
record.gate_note: The study reports pretraining-loss scaling fits, larger-model perplexities, and downstream GLUE results. Tokenizer-selection values and ICER values are not rows: they are used to choose or compare configuration settings, rather than reporting the claimed scaling behaviour itself.
record.test_reason: The study fits power curves to MLM pretraining loss against data size, model size and FLOPs for 1–100M-parameter encoders on reduced-vocabulary text. It argues explicitly that the FLOPs power law breaks below about 2.2×10^15 FLOPs and that parameter count does not reliably predict loss. It also correlates pretraining perplexity with GLUE scores. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. With a reduced vocabulary, pretraining benefits show up from 1.25M parameters, and filtered-GLUE score correlates strongly with perplexity (unfiltered GLUE does not). Compute-optimal pretraining does not appear crucial downstream, and parameter count does not reliably predict MLM loss. The FLOPs–perplexity power law breaks at about 2.2×10^15 FLOPs. Adding layers does not always help GLUE, and fewer layers (2–4) did best.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses masked-language-modeling Transformer encoders, reduced-vocabulary text, and loss/perplexity fits on compute-optimal instances. The original scaling-law studies use different model and training setups; this paper describes its MLM loss and reduced-vocabulary language as reasons its exponents differ.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling relation changes by FLOPs region: the fit is strong above 2^15 FLOPs but weak and discontinuous in the low-FLOPs region. Filtered versus unfiltered GLUE also changes the observed perplexity–downstream correlation.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed configuration and token count, training on unconstrained text rather than reduced-vocabulary text raises the parameter count (up to +5.13M) and FLOPs (+33–52%). It also worsens constrained-test perplexity (+15–26%) and filtered GLUE (up to −20%) for models of ≤22M parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For very small models, restricting vocabulary/language size improves loss and downstream performance per parameter.

fits_no_version.finding: Every pretrained configuration beats its randomly initialised counterpart on filtered GLUE, down to 1.25M parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining benefits on downstream tasks appear in models as small as ~1M parameters when the language is reduced.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2023)
record.problems: The models are masked-language-modeling encoders trained on reduced-vocabulary text, limiting generality to other setups. The authors describe low R² values for model-size and data-size fits, and note that larger-model results may be limited by insufficient training data. The reported scaling fits use the development set, whereas test perplexity is reported separately.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were made for every configuration in Figures 2 and 3: the text supplies aggregate fit statistics, while individual plotted points are not numerically stated. Other GLUE configurations and the unconstrained-language comparisons are not included because the selected rows already capture the reported correlation and the depth-related variation relevant to the tested versions.

untested.parts: Causal decoder LMs, unrestricted vocabulary, models above ~100M parameters, and whether the fits span several orders of magnitude. The FLOPs range is not stated numerically.
No forecast from small fits is checked against larger runs.
There is no fit of loss-minimising N or D as a function of compute. The claim 'data and model scaling equally important' is an inference from similar loss exponents only.
Only head count is varied at exactly fixed parameter count. Depth/width trade-offs are only at approximately matched counts and are not row-recorded.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling law is fitted.
Fitting method, parameter counting and schedule are not varied. Exponent differences from Kaplan are noted but not tested.

missing.what: Pretraining perplexity for all Table 3 configurations. These show depth/width effects at near-equal parameter counts, e.g. 1 layer at 10.71M gives 7.60 vs 5.88 for H=128 at 10.04M, and I=512 at 9.20M gives 5.12.
GLUE vs model size and FLOPs for 27 compute-optimal and non-compute-optimal checkpoints. Compute-optimal models do not necessarily do better downstream at a given parameter count.

The authors' statement that similar N and D exponents (−0.2805, −0.2459) mean data and model scaling are 'equally important for compute-optimality'. This is an indirect inference; no N_opt(C) fit is reported, so no V3 verdict is given.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'reversed' states for r5–r11 are not supported. The 4.67 reference comes from a different configuration family, and the authors attribute the plateau to insufficient data, which V1 already excludes. Within the larger-model set, loss falls monotonically with size, so no V1 verdict is drawn from these rows. The '2^15' in r3 mirrors a typo in the paper. Learning rates differ by model size (>18M parameters vs smaller), which also confounds the r5–r11 comparison. The setting is MLM encoders on filtered text with a single seed, and the FLOPs range covered is not stated numerically.

versions.untested_parts: The results concern masked-language-modeling encoders on reduced-vocabulary text at small scale; they do not test general language-model setups or the full range of several orders of magnitude.
The study does not fit curves on small runs and compare their forecasts with observed losses of substantially larger runs.

The study does not report fitted curves for the loss-minimising parameter count and token count as functions of compute. It fits loss against model and data size among compute-optimal instances instead.
The controlled fixed-parameter-count comparison varies attention-head count; it does not isolate depth, width, and all other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime such as image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling is tested as a power law.
Downstream predictability is evaluated on filtered and unfiltered GLUE; the study does not test downstream tasks beyond those benchmarks.
The study reports bending at low compute and fit results in its setup, but does not systematically vary fitting choices or compare alternative parameter-counting, schedules, or datasets.
